claim: Cryptococcus neoformans causes over 180,000 deaths each year from cryptococcal meningitis.
source: There are over 278,000 cases of cryptococcal meningitis every year, causing over 180,000 deaths (Rajasingham et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rajasingham et al., 2017

claim: There are over 278,000 cases of cryptococcal meningitis every year.
source: There are over 278,000 cases of cryptococcal meningitis every year, causing over 180,000 deaths (Rajasingham et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rajasingham et al., 2017

claim: Cryptococcal meningitis is primarily caused by the ubiquitous environmental fungus Cryptococcus neoformans.
source: Cryptococcal meningitis is primarily caused by the ubiquitous environmental fungus Cryptococcus neoformans.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: Airborne spores or desiccated yeast cells of C. neoformans are inhaled into the lungs, where they are cleared or remain dormant until reactivation upon host immunosuppression.
source: Airborne spores or desiccated yeast cells of C. neoformans are inhaled into the lungs, where they are cleared or remain dormant until reactivation upon host immunosuppression (Casadevall and Perfect, 1998; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Casadevall and Perfect, 1998 and Zhao et al., 2019

claim: Most environmental Cryptococcus isolates cannot cause fatal disease in mouse models of cryptococcosis, despite having similar genotypes and in vitro phenotypes to known virulent isolates.
source: Litvintseva et al. found that most environmental Cryptococcus isolates cannot cause fatal disease in mouse models of cryptococcosis, despite having similar genotypes and in vitro phenotypes to known virulent isolates, including thermotolerance, melanization, and capsule production (Litvintseva and Mitchell, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Litvintseva and Mitchell, 2009

claim: In vitro phenotype assays for thermotolerance, capsule production, titan cell formation, or fluconazole heteroresistance could not differentiate high-virulence strains from low-virulence strains.
source: Mukaremera et al., 2019 also observed that in vitro phenotype assays for thermotolerance, capsule production, titan cell formation, or fluconazole heteroresistance could not differentiate high-virulence strains from low-virulence strains.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukaremera et al., 2019

claim: Tolerance to host levels of CO2 (~5% CO2 in the host vs. ~0.04% in ambient air) is likely a significant factor separating potentially virulent natural isolates from non-pathogenic environmental isolates.
source: Tolerance to host levels of CO2 (~5% CO2 in the host vs. ~0.04% in ambient air) is likely a significant factor separating the potentially virulent natural isolates from the non-pathogenic environmental isolates that Litvintseva et al. tested (Krysan et al., 2019; Litvintseva and Mitchell, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krysan et al., 2019 and Litvintseva and Mitchell, 2009

claim: Many genes have been shown to be essential for thermotolerance in C. neoformans, including calcineurin.
source: Many genes have been shown to be essential for thermotolerance (Perfect, 2006; Stempinski et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2017), including calcineurin which is currently being explored for antifungal drug development (Gobeil et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Perfect, 2006; Stempinski et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2017; and Gobeil et al., 2021

claim: Calcineurin is currently being explored for antifungal drug development.
source: Many genes have been shown to be essential for thermotolerance (Perfect, 2006; Stempinski et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2017), including calcineurin which is currently being explored for antifungal drug development (Gobeil et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gobeil et al., 2021

claim: The underlying mechanisms or genes that play a role in CO2 tolerance have yet to be identified in C. neoformans.
source: By contrast, the underlying mechanisms or genes that play a role in CO2 tolerance have yet to be identified.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Many C. neoformans environmental strains are sensitive to 5% CO2 when grown on buffered RPMI media.
source: Our previous work indicates that many C. neoformans environmental strains are sensitive to 5% CO2 when grown on buffered RPMI media, commonly used for mammalian cell cultures and testing antifungal susceptibility (Krysan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krysan et al., 2019

claim: CO2 at host concentrations acts synergistically with fluconazole in inhibiting cryptococcal growth on buffered RPMI media.
source: CO2 at host concentrations also acts synergistically with the commonly used antifungal drug fluconazole in inhibiting cryptococcal growth on buffered RPMI media.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krysan et al., 2019 in the previous sentence

claim: Clearance zones were much larger in 5% CO2 relative to those in ambient air at both pH 6 and pH 7, indicating that CO2 sensitizes cryptococcal susceptibility to fluconazole.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, clearance zones were much larger in 5% CO2 relative to those in ambient air at both pH 6 and pH 7, indicating that CO2 sensitizes cryptococcal susceptibility to fluconazole.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: CO2 inhibits the growth of H99 at both pH 6 and pH 7.
source: Furthermore, CO2 inhibits the growth of H99 at both pH 6 and pH 7 (smaller colony size in 5% CO2 relative to that in ambient air).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation in Figure 1A

claim: Growth of CO2-sensitive environmental strain A7-35-23 was severely inhibited by 5% CO2 at both pH 6 and pH 7.
source: Additionally, growth of CO2-sensitive environmental strain A7-35-23 (Krysan et al., 2019) was severely inhibited by 5% CO2 at both pH 6 and pH 7 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Krysan et al., 2019

claim: C. neoformans grows better at acidic pH and can grow well in pH 3.
source: In general, C. neoformans grows better at acidic pH (can grow well in pH 3), and both A7-35-23 and H99 grew better at pH 6 than at pH 7 in ambient air (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and general knowledge

claim: Cryptococcal growth inhibition by CO2 is not simply due to lowered pH.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that cryptococcal growth inhibition by CO2 is not simply due to lowered pH.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing CO2 inhibition at both pH 6 and pH 7

claim: 96 gene knockout mutants out of over 5000 screened were found to be sensitive to CO2.
source: From over 5000 gene knockout mutants screened (~7000 protein coding genes in the H99 genome), 96 were found to be sensitive to CO2 by visual observation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental screening data

claim: Knockout mutants for multiple pathways known to be activated by heat stress are CO2 sensitive, including the Ras1-Cdc24 pathway, calcineurin, cell wall integrity (CWI), and Regulator of Ace2 and Morphogenesis (RAM).
source: We noticed that knockout mutants for multiple pathways known to be activated by heat stress are CO2 sensitive, including the Ras1-Cdc24 pathway, calcineurin, cell wall integrity (CWI), and Regulator of Ace2 and Morphogenesis (RAM).
evidence: Supported by experimental screening data

claim: There is an overlapping nature between CO2 tolerance and thermotolerance.
source: This finding indicates an overlapping nature of these two traits.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heat stress pathways are also CO2 sensitive

claim: Adenylyl cyclase pathway mutants showed no growth defects at host levels CO2, including cac1Δ, aca1Δ, gpa1Δ, and pkr1Δ.
source: However, we found that adenylyl cyclase pathway mutants showed no growth defects at host levels CO2, including the adenylyl cyclase mutant cac1Δ, the adenylyl cyclase associated protein mutant aca1Δ, the alpha G protein subunit mutant gpa1Δ, and the cAMP-dependent protein kinase mutant pkr1Δ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Growth defects in response to host levels of CO2 are likely independent of bicarbonate activation of adenylyl cyclase.
source: This indicates that growth defects in response to host levels of CO2 are likely independent of bicarbonate activation of adenylyl cyclase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that adenylyl cyclase pathway mutants show no CO2 growth defects

claim: Bicarbonate is not a limiting factor under the high level of CO2 used in the screen.
source: This is not unexpected given that bicarbonate is not a limiting factor under the high level of CO2 used in our screen.
evidence: Based on knowledge of bicarbonate chemistry at high CO2 levels

claim: The cbk1Δ mutant showed the most severe defect in thermotolerance and CO2 tolerance compared to mutants of other pathways.
source: As the RAM pathway effector kinase mutant cbk1Δ showed the most severe defect in thermotolerance and CO2 tolerance compared to the mutants of the other pathways, we first overexpressed the gene CBK1 in the following mutants, cdc24Δ (Ras1-Cdc24), mpk1Δ (CWI), cna1Δ (Calcineurin), and the cbk1Δ mutant itself and observed their growth at host temperature and host CO2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Overexpression of CBK1 largely restored the growth defects of the cbk1Δ mutant at 37°C with and without 5% CO2.
source: As expected, the growth defects of the cbk1Δ mutant at 37°C with and without 5% CO2 were largely restored by CBK1 overexpression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Overexpression of CBK1 restored the growth of mpk1Δ, cna1Δ, and cdc24Δ mutants in the CO2 condition at 30°C.
source: At 30°C, overexpression of CBK1 restored the growth of the mpk1Δ mutant, the cna1Δ mutant, and the cdc24Δ mutant in the CO2 condition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Overexpression of CBK1 restored growth of mpk1Δ but not cna1Δ in terms of thermotolerance.
source: In terms of thermotolerance, overexpression of CBK1 restored growth of mpk1Δ but not cna1Δ, while the growth defect of cdc24Δ at 37°C was exacerbated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The growth defect of cdc24Δ at 37°C was exacerbated by CBK1 overexpression.
source: In terms of thermotolerance, overexpression of CBK1 restored growth of mpk1Δ but not cna1Δ, while the growth defect of cdc24Δ at 37°C was exacerbated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: CBK1 overexpression failed to rescue growth of tested CO2-sensitive mutants when both temperature and CO2 stressors were present (37°C+5% CO2).
source: CBK1 overexpression failed to rescue growth of any of these mutants when both stressors were present (37°C+5% CO2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Overexpression of CBK1 in the WT H99 background caused a modest growth defect at 37°C+5% CO2.
source: We found that overexpression of CBK1 in the WT H99 background caused a modest growth defect at 37°C+5% CO2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Overexpression of CDC24, MPK1, or CNA1 in the cbk1Δ mutant background did not restore growth under 37°C and/or 5% CO2.
source: The reciprocal overexpression of CDC24, MPK1, or CNA1 in the cbk1Δ mutant background did not restore growth under 37°C and/or 5% CO2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Cbk1 integrates multiple stress response pathways to regulate both CO2 tolerance and thermotolerance.
source: These results support a hypothesis that Cbk1 integrates multiple stress response pathways to regulate both CO2 tolerance and thermotolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing CBK1 overexpression effects on multiple pathway mutants

claim: 81 out of 118 CO2-associated genes were found to be significantly differentially expressed in the cbk1Δ mutant in both ambient air and in 5% CO2.
source: Out of these 118 CO2-associated genes, 81 were found to be significantly differentially expressed in the cbk1Δ mutant in both ambient air and in 5% CO2, indicating they are intrinsically dysregulated in the cbk1Δ mutant.
evidence: Supported by NanoString gene expression profiling data shown in Figure 2C

claim: 57 out of 81 differentially expressed genes in cbk1Δ are downregulated and 24 out of 81 are upregulated compared to the WT H99 strain.
source: 57/81 of these genes are downregulated and 24/81 upregulated compared to the WT H99 strain (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by NanoString gene expression profiling data shown in Figure 2D

claim: 16 out of 57 downregulated genes in cbk1Δ were also hits in the deletion set screening.
source: Interestingly, 16/57 of the downregulated genes were also hits in our deletion set screening.
evidence: Supported by comparison of NanoString data with screening results

claim: Loss of Cbk1 significantly affects the expression of CO2-related genes.
source: Taken together, this transcriptomic profiling shows that loss of Cbk1 significantly affects the expression of CO2-related genes.
evidence: Supported by NanoString gene expression profiling data

claim: The RAM pathway effector kinase Cbk1 is part of the NDR/LATS family of kinases, which is conserved from yeast to humans.
source: The RAM pathway effector kinase Cbk1 is part of the NDR/LATS family of kinases, which is conserved from yeast to humans and affects a wide range of cellular functions including cell-cycle regulation.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: Deletion of CBK1 impacts various virulence factors in C. neoformans, including urease activity and thermotolerance.
source: In C. neoformans, various virulence factors are impacted by deletion of CBK1, including urease activity and thermotolerance (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2016

claim: All tested Cryptococcus RAM pathway mutants are extremely sensitive to 5% CO2 and high temperature, and they show no growth at 37°C+5% CO2.
source: Through our genetic screen for CO2-sensitive mutants, we found that all tested Cryptococcus RAM pathway mutants are extremely sensitive to 5% CO2 and high temperature, and they show no growth at 37°C+5% CO2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: In ascomycetes such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and C. albicans, RAM pathway mutants are defective in cytokinesis and exhibit loss of polarity, resulting in enlarged round cells that cluster together.
source: In ascomycetes such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and C. albicans, RAM pathway mutants are defective in cytokinesis and exhibit loss of polarity, resulting in enlarged round cells that cluster together (Saputo et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saputo et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Cryptococcus RAM pathway mutants are hyper-polarized and constitutively form clusters of elongated pseudohyphal cells.
source: In contrast, though defective in cytokinesis (Magditch et al., 2012; Walton et al., 2006), Cryptococcus RAM pathway mutants are hyper-polarized and constitutively form clusters of elongated pseudohyphal cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Magditch et al., 2012 and Walton et al., 2006

claim: Cryptococcus RAM pathway mutants are defective in cytokinesis.
source: In contrast, though defective in cytokinesis (Magditch et al., 2012; Walton et al., 2006), Cryptococcus RAM pathway mutants are hyper-polarized and constitutively form clusters of elongated pseudohyphal cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Magditch et al., 2012 and Walton et al., 2006

claim: The C. albicans homozygous cbk1ΔΔ mutant exhibits a general growth defect compared to the WT control but shows no apparent specific growth defect at 37°C with or without 5% CO2.
source: Moreover, we found that while the C. albicans homozygous cbk1ΔΔ mutant exhibits a general growth defect compared to the WT control, it shows no apparent specific growth defect at 37°C with or without 5% CO2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Although the RAM pathway is conserved in its role in cytokinesis, the effects of its downstream targets are divergent between ascomycetes and basidiomycetes.
source: These results suggest that, although the RAM pathway is conserved in its role in cytokinesis, the effects of its downstream targets are divergent between ascomycetes and basidiomycetes.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in RAM pathway mutant phenotypes between ascomycetes and basidiomycetes

claim: In ascomycetes, Ace2 is a key downstream transcription factor of the RAM pathway, which is important for the activation of genes responsible for cell separation.
source: In ascomycetes, Ace2 is a key downstream transcription factor of the RAM pathway (hence in the name of RAM − Regulator of Ace2 and Morphogenesis), which is important for the activation of genes responsible for cell separation as well as a large number of genes with other functions (Mulhern et al., 2006; Wakade et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mulhern et al., 2006 and Wakade et al., 2020

claim: No homolog to Ace2 has been identified in Cryptococcus or other basidiomycetes.
source: However, no homolog to Ace2 has been identified in Cryptococcus or other basidiomycetes.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap based on bioinformatics analysis

claim: No downstream targets of the RAM pathway have been identified in any basidiomycetes.
source: Furthermore, no downstream targets of the RAM pathway have been identified in any basidiomycetes.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Out of >1×10^8 cbk1Δ cells plated and cultured at 37°C+5% CO2, 11 suppressor colonies were isolated.
source: Out of >1×108 cells plated and cultured under this condition that is inhibitory for growth of the original cbk1Δ mutant, 11 suppressor colonies were isolated for further examination and sequencing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from suppressor screening

claim: All the suppressor isolates showed dramatically improved growth over the original cbk1Δ mutant at 37°C and modestly improved growth at 37°C+5% CO2.
source: All the suppressor isolates showed dramatically improved growth over the original cbk1Δ mutant at 37°C and modestly improved growth at 37°C+5% CO2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The 11 suppressors were classified into two groups: sup1 (2/11) and sup2 (9/11).
source: Based on their distinctive phenotypes, the 11 suppressors were classified into two groups: sup1 (2/11) and sup2 (9/11).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and classification

claim: Shorter chains of cells in both suppressor groups indicate a partial restoration in cytokinesis.
source: Shorter chains of cells in both groups indicate a partial restoration in cytokinesis (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The sup2 group has slightly improved growth at 37°C+5% CO2 and forms shorter chains of cells compared to the sup1 group.
source: The sup2 group has slightly improved growth at 37°C+5% CO2 and forms shorter chains of cells compared to the sup1 group (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: Both sup1 and sup2 displayed similar phenotypes in growth assays including melanin production, capsule, urease activity, and cell wall stress tolerance.
source: Besides of these observations, sup1 and sup2 displayed similar phenotypes in growth assays including the cryptococcal virulence traits tested, including melanin production, capsule, urease activity, and cell wall stress tolerance. (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Both sup1 and sup2 showed no improved growth compared to the cbk1Δ mutant at pH 7.4 37°C+5% CO2.
source: Both sup1 and sup2 showed no improved growth compared to the cbk1Δ mutant at pH 7.4 37°C+5% CO2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Both sup1 and sup2 failed to restore growth of the cbk1Δ on media supplemented with FK506 or restore the ability to mate with the congenic strain H99a.
source: We found that both sup1 and sup2 failed to restore growth of the cbk1Δ on media supplemented with FK506 or restore the ability to mate with the congenic strain H99a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Both sup1 type suppressor mutants contained a disruptive in-frame deletion at the same location in CNAG_01919, which encodes a putative Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) domain-containing protein.
source: By comparing their genome sequences with each other and with the original cbk1Δ mutant, we found that both sup1 type suppressor mutants contained a disruptive in-frame deletion at the same location in CNAG_01919, which encodes a putative Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) domain-containing protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data

claim: The PARN domain was previously reported in S. pombe proteins.
source: This domain was previously reported in S. pombe proteins (Marasovic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marasovic et al., 2013

claim: The PARN domain is not present in any protein in the genomes of S. cerevisiae, C. albicans, or other ascomycetes but is found in basidiomycetes and higher eukaryotes.
source: Interestingly, through a BLAST search of the PARN domain, we did not identify this domain in any protein in the genomes of S. cerevisiae, C. albicans, or other ascomycetes but found it in basidiomycetes and higher eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis using BLAST

claim: The in-frame deletion in PSC1 results in a change of two amino acids within the predicted PARN domain.
source: The in-frame deletion results in a change of two amino acids within the predicted PARN domain, the only discernable domain present in this protein.
evidence: Supported by genome sequencing and protein analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: All nine sup2 isolates contained loss of function or missense mutations in the gene CNAG_03345, which encodes an RNA-binding protein homologous to S. cerevisiae Ssd1p.
source: All nine sup2 isolates contained loss of function or missense mutations in the gene CNAG_03345 (Figure 4B), which encodes an RNA-binding protein homologous to S. cerevisiae Ssd1p, a known suppressor of cbk1Δ phenotypes in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4B

claim: S. cerevisiae Ssd1p is a known suppressor of cbk1Δ phenotypes in S. cerevisiae.
source: All nine sup2 isolates contained loss of function or missense mutations in the gene CNAG_03345 (Figure 4B), which encodes an RNA-binding protein homologous to S. cerevisiae Ssd1p, a known suppressor of cbk1Δ phenotypes in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: ScSsd1p represses transcript translation and is negatively regulated by Cbk1p phosphorylation.
source: ScSsd1p represses transcript translation and is negatively regulated by Cbk1p phosphorylation (Jansen et al., 2009; Wanless et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jansen et al., 2009 and Wanless et al., 2014

claim: Relative to the cbk1Δ mutant, the cbk1Δssd1Δ and cbk1Δpsc1Δ double mutants showed reduced sensitivity to host temperature and CO2 levels.
source: Indeed, relative to the cbk1Δ mutant, the double mutants showed reduced sensitivity to host temperature and CO2 levels (Figure 4C), similar to the natural suppressor mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The morphology of the cbk1Δssd1Δ and cbk1Δpsc1Δ double mutants resembles that of the spontaneous suppressor mutants.
source: Likewise, the morphology of the double mutants resembles that of the spontaneous suppressor mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The deletion of SSD1 and PSC1 alone in the WT background did not yield any discernable phenotype.
source: The deletion of SSD1 and PSC1 alone in the WT background did not yield any discernable phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in SSD1 and PSC1 are responsible for partial suppression of the cbk1Δ mutant's growth defects.
source: The results confirm that loss-of-function mutations in SSD1 and PSC1 are responsible for partial suppression of the cbk1Δ mutant's growth defects observed in the isolated suppressor strains.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from double mutant construction and phenotypic analysis

claim: sup2 and the cbk1Δssd1Δ mutants both grew noticeably better than sup1 and cbk1Δpsc1Δ at 37°C and 37°C+5% CO2.
source: Interestingly, sup2 and the cbk1Δssd1Δ mutants both grew noticeably better than sup1 and cbk1Δpsc1Δ at 37°C and 37°C+5% CO2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The psc1Δssd1Δ control strain did not exhibit any defect and grew similarly well to either single mutant or the WT.
source: The psc1Δssd1Δ control strain did not exhibit any defect and grew similarly well to either single mutant or the WT (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The triple mutant cbk1Δpsc1Δssd1Δ grew similarly well as sup2 or cbk1Δssd1Δ at 37°C+5% CO2.
source: The triple mutant cbk1Δpsc1Δssd1Δ grew similarly well as sup2 or cbk1Δssd1Δ at 37°C+5% CO2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The triple mutant cbk1Δpsc1Δssd1Δ displayed aberrant morphology and budding defects which are not observed in the natural suppressor mutants or the cbk1Δssd1Δ and cbk1Δpsc1Δ double mutants.
source: However, the triple mutant displayed aberrant morphology and budding defects which are not observed in the natural suppressor mutants or the cbk1Δssd1Δ and cbk1Δpsc1Δ double mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Psc1 and Ssd1 may function in the same pathway in regulating thermotolerance and CO2 tolerance.
source: These results suggest that Psc1 and Ssd1 may function in the same pathway in regulating thermotolerance and CO2 tolerance, but their downstream effects on cell separation and/or polarized growth may be overlapping and distinct.
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction analysis of double and triple mutants

claim: The downstream effects of Psc1 and Ssd1 on cell separation and/or polarized growth may be overlapping and distinct.
source: These results suggest that Psc1 and Ssd1 may function in the same pathway in regulating thermotolerance and CO2 tolerance, but their downstream effects on cell separation and/or polarized growth may be overlapping and distinct.
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction analysis showing different morphological phenotypes

claim: The spontaneous suppressors do not restore transcript abundances of most differentially expressed genes in cbk1Δ to WT levels.
source: Overall, we found that the spontaneous suppressors do not restore transcript abundances of most differentially expressed genes in cbk1Δ to WT levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that suppressors affect post-transcriptional regulation of CO2 tolerance.
evidence: Supported by NanoString gene expression profiling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Suppressors affect post-transcriptional regulation of CO2 tolerance.
source: Overall, we found that the spontaneous suppressors do not restore transcript abundances of most differentially expressed genes in cbk1Δ to WT levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that suppressors affect post-transcriptional regulation of CO2 tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transcript levels are not restored despite phenotypic rescue

claim: RAM mutants have previously been found to be attenuated in virulence in the invertebrate wax moth larva infection model and mouse intranasal infection models.
source: RAM mutants have previously been found to be attenuated in virulence in the invertebrate wax moth larva infection model and mouse intranasal infection models (Lee et al., 2016; Magditch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2016 and Magditch et al., 2012

claim: Occasionally, cryptococcal strains with point mutations in RAM genes cause death of mice when revertant mutations occur, which restore the function of the RAM pathway.
source: Occasionally, cryptococcal strains with point mutations in RAM genes cause death of mice when revertant mutations occur, which restore the function of the RAM pathway (Magditch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Magditch et al., 2012

claim: All mice infected with H99 were moribund by day 26 post-infection.
source: As expected, all mice infected with H99 were moribund by DPI 26 (Figure 5A), while those infected with the cbk1Δ mutant survived until the experiment was terminated at DPI 60.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Mice infected with the cbk1Δ mutant survived until the experiment was terminated at day 60 post-infection.
source: As expected, all mice infected with H99 were moribund by DPI 26 (Figure 5A), while those infected with the cbk1Δ mutant survived until the experiment was terminated at DPI 60.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: sup1 and sup2 strains did not cause any mortality in the intranasal infection model.
source: Surprisingly, sup1 and sup2 strains did not cause any mortality either.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: At the time of euthanasia for H99-infected mice (prior to day 26 post-infection), the median fungal burden in the lungs, brains, and kidneys was 2.1×10^8, 1.4×10^6, and 2.4×10^4 colony-forming units (CFUs) per organ, respectively.
source: At the time of euthanasia for H99-infected mice (prior to DPI 26), the median fungal burden in the lungs, brains, and kidneys was 2.1×108, 1.4×106, and 2.4×104 colony-forming units (CFUs) per organ, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Mice completely cleared the cbk1Δ mutant at day 35 post-infection.
source: As expected, mice completely cleared the cbk1Δ mutant at DPI 35.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: sup1 was completely cleared from the mouse lungs by day 35 post-infection, similar to the cbk1Δ mutant.
source: Surprisingly, despite largely restored growth at 37°C, sup1 was completely cleared from the mouse lungs by DPI 35, similar to the cbk1Δ mutant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: sup2 was able to replicate in the mouse lungs with a median lung fungal burden at day 35 post-infection of 8.2×10^4, over eightfold higher than the original inoculum.
source: In comparison, although sup2 did not cause any death during the study period, it was able to replicate in the mouse lungs. The median lung fungal burden at DPI 35 was 8.2×104, over eightfold higher than the original inoculum.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The sup2 strain maintained the same high lung fungal burden at day 60 post-infection, indicating that it can persist in the lung tissue.
source: The sup2 strain maintained the same high lung fungal burden at DPI 60 (Figure 5B), indicating that it can persist in the lung tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: No fungal burden was detected in the brain or the kidney for sup2 at day 35 or 60 post-infection, indicating that the mutant was unable to disseminate.
source: Although the spontaneous suppressor sup2 was able to replicate in the mouse lungs, no fungal burden was detected in the brain or the kidney at DPI 35 or 60 (no organisms were detected in any of the mice), indicating that the mutant was unable to disseminate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: C. neoformans can disseminate from the lungs to other organs by a 'Trojan Horse' mechanism, where Cryptococcus travels within the mobile host phagocytes.
source: Because C. neoformans can disseminate from the lungs to other organs by a 'Trojan Horse' mechanism, where Cryptococcus travels within the mobile host phagocytes (Kechichian et al., 2007; Santiago-Tirado et al., 2017), we examined phagocytosis of the cbk1Δ mutant and its suppressors to test the first hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kechichian et al., 2007 and Santiago-Tirado et al., 2017

claim: The cbk1Δ mutant was previously found to have a poor phagocytosis index.
source: We expected that cryptococcal mutants defective in being phagocytosed by host cells might be defective in dissemination, and the cbk1Δ mutant was previously found to have a poor phagocytosis index (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2015

claim: Phagocytosis of the cbk1Δ mutant was extremely low (~1% of the WT H99 level under complement mediated phagocytosis).
source: Consistent with our previous finding, phagocytosis of the cbk1Δ mutant was extremely low (~1% of the WT H99 level under complement mediated phagocytosis, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Opsonization with serum from vaccinated mice increased phagocytosis of cbk1Δ and the suppressor mutants, but the phagocytosis indexes of these mutants were still only 20% or less than that of the WT.
source: Opsonization with serum from vaccinated mice increased phagocytosis of cbk1Δ and the suppressor mutants, but the phagocytosis indexes of these mutants were still only 20% or less than that of the WT (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The suppressor mutants or the double mutants cbk1∆ssd1∆ and cbk1∆psc1∆ mutants showed increased phagocytosis relative to the cbk1∆ mutant in both phagocytosis experiments.
source: In both phagocytosis experiments, the suppressor mutants or the double mutants cbk1∆ssd1∆ and cbk1∆psc1∆ mutants showed increased phagocytosis relative to the cbk1∆ mutant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D

claim: The poor phagocytosis of the cbk1Δ mutant and its suppressors may contribute to their lack of dissemination from the lungs to the other organs in the inhalation infection mouse model of cryptococcosis.
source: The poor phagocytosis of the cbk1Δ mutant and its suppressors may contribute to their lack of dissemination from the lungs to the other organs in the inhalation infection mouse model of cryptococcosis.
evidence: Inferred from the phagocytosis data and dissemination results

claim: H99 cells disseminate to the brain and other organs within hours in the intravenous infection model.
source: In this intravenous infection model, the barrier of the lungs is bypassed. H99 cells disseminate to the brain and other organs within hours (O'Connor et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Connor et al., 2013

claim: H99-infected mice showed high fungal burdens in the lungs, brains, and kidneys at day 5 post-infection in the intravenous model, with the highest fungal burden in the brain (over 10^6 CFUs).
source: As expected, H99-infected mice showed high fungal burdens in the lungs, brains, and kidneys, with the highest fungal burden in the brain (over 106 CFUs; Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: The cbk1Δ mutant failed to disseminate in the intravenous infection model as no viable cells were recovered in any organ.
source: The cbk1Δ mutant failed to disseminate in this intravenous infection model as no viable cells were recovered in any organ.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: No sup1 cells were recovered from the lungs or the brain and only a few fungal cells were detected in the kidney in the intravenous infection model.
source: Similarly, we could not recover any sup1 cells from the lungs or the brain and only detected a few fungal cells in the kidney.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: sup2 suppressor mutants were recovered in all three organs in the intravenous infection model, albeit with reduced fungal burdens (~10^4 CFUs in the brain and a few hundred in lungs/kidney) compared to the WT H99 control group.
source: In contrast, sup2 suppressor mutants were recovered in all three organs, albeit with reduced fungal burdens (~104 CFUs in the brain and a few hundred in lungs/kidney) compared to the WT H99 control group (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: The sup2 suppressor, once disseminated into the bloodstream, can invade other organs and replicate.
source: This finding indicates that the sup2 suppressor, once disseminated into the bloodstream, can invade other organs and replicate.
evidence: Inferred from the intravenous infection data showing sup2 recovery in multiple organs

claim: The observation that only sup2 can survive, amplify, and persist in animals implicates an importance of CO2 tolerance in cryptococcal pathogenesis.
source: Combined with the earlier observations that (1) both suppressors fully restore growth at host temperature and (2) sup2 is slightly more CO2 tolerant than sup1, the observation that only sup2 can survive, amplify, and persist in animals implicates an importance of CO2 tolerance in cryptococcal pathogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental results

claim: Failure of the suppressor mutants to disseminate to other organs in the intranasal model is largely due to reduced phagocytosis and inability to escape the lungs.
source: Collectively, the results from phagocytosis, the inhalation infection model, and the intravenous infection model support the hypothesis that failure of the suppressor mutants to disseminate to other organs in the intranasal model is largely due to reduced phagocytosis and inability to escape the lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of phagocytosis assays and infection models

claim: The cbk1Δssd1Δ mutant recapitulated the phenotype of the sup2 strain in intravenous infection model and other in vitro assays.
source: Again, the cbk1Δssd1Δ mutant recapitulated the phenotype of the sup2 strain in intravenous infection model and other in vitro assays, demonstrating that our observed sup2 phenotypes are due to disruption of SSD1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and other assays

claim: All 20 of the larvae inoculated with the H99 strain died between day 3 and day 10 post-inoculation in the G. mellonella infection model.
source: All 20 of the larvae inoculated with the H99 strain died between DPI 3 and DPI 10 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Only 2/20 of the cbk1Δ mutant-infected larvae died during the 15-day period in the G. mellonella infection model.
source: In comparison, only 2/20 of the cbk1Δ mutant-infected larvae died during this period.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: 5/20 sup1-infected larvae and 7/20 sup2-infected larvae died in the G. mellonella infection experiment, indicating their partially restored virulence in this larva infection model.
source: Interestingly, 5/20 sup1-infected larvae and 7/20 sup2-infected larvae died in this experiment (Figure 6A), indicating their partially restored virulence in this larva infection model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: At day 5 post-inoculation in G. mellonella, the mean fungal burden of WT-infected larvae was 1.5×10^7 CFUs.
source: At DPI 5, the mean fungal burden of WT-infected larvae was 1.5×107 CFUs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The mean fungal burden for the cbk1Δ-infected larvae at day 5 post-inoculation was only 8.4×10^2 CFUs, which is almost 20,000-fold lower than the WT control group and about 60-fold lower than the original inoculum.
source: In comparison, the mean fungal burden for the cbk1Δ-infected larvae was only 8.4×102 CFUs, which is almost 20,000-fold lower than the WT control group and about 60-fold lower than the original inoculum, indicating that most cbk1Δ cells have been cleared by this time point.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The mean fungal burden of sup1-infected larvae at day 5 post-inoculation was 9.6×10^3 CFUs.
source: The mean fungal burden of sup1-infected larvae was 9.6×103 CFUs, while the mean fungal burden sup2-infected larvae was 2.3×104 CFUs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The mean fungal burden of sup2-infected larvae at day 5 post-inoculation was 2.3×10^4 CFUs.
source: The mean fungal burden of sup1-infected larvae was 9.6×103 CFUs, while the mean fungal burden sup2-infected larvae was 2.3×104 CFUs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Both sup1 and sup2 partially rescued virulence of the cbk1Δ mutant in the G. mellonella insect model.
source: These results indicate that both sup1 and sup2 partially rescued virulence of the cbk1Δ mutant and that sup2 showed slightly better restoration of virulence compared to sup1 in this insect model, which is independent of tolerance to mammalian body temperature.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B

claim: sup2 showed slightly better restoration of virulence compared to sup1 in the G. mellonella insect model, which is independent of tolerance to mammalian body temperature.
source: These results indicate that both sup1 and sup2 partially rescued virulence of the cbk1Δ mutant and that sup2 showed slightly better restoration of virulence compared to sup1 in this insect model, which is independent of tolerance to mammalian body temperature.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B

claim: Detection of and adaptation to changing CO2 levels are an important trait across biological kingdoms and may play a crucial role in the pathogenicity of fungi.
source: Detection of and adaptation to changing CO2 levels are an important trait across biological kingdoms and may play a crucial role in the pathogenicity of fungi (Bahn and Mühlschlegel, 2006; Cummins et al., 2014; Hetherington and Raven, 2005; Krysan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bahn and Mühlschlegel, 2006; Cummins et al., 2014; Hetherington and Raven, 2005; and Krysan et al., 2019

claim: Growth in response to host CO2 may be intricately coordinated and co-regulated with response to host temperature.
source: Multiple pathways important for growth at high temperature, such as the Ras1-Cdc24, CWI, Calcineurin, and RAM pathways, were found to be required for growth in high CO2 concentrations, indicating that growth in response to host CO2 may be intricately coordinated and co-regulated with response to host temperature.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental finding that heat stress pathways are required for CO2 tolerance

claim: Both host CO2 and host temperature represent stressors that cryptococcal cells infecting mammalian hosts must overcome to cause disease.
source: It is therefore likely that both host CO2 and host temperature represent stressors that cryptococcal cells infecting mammalian hosts must overcome to cause disease.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing overlapping pathways for CO2 and temperature tolerance

claim: A previous study found synthetic lethality between the RAM and calcineurin pathways in C. neoformans but not in S. cerevisiae.
source: A previous study found synthetic lethality between the RAM and calcineurin pathways in C. neoformans but not in S. cerevisiae (Walton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walton et al., 2006

claim: In C. albicans, CO2 levels are sensed through bicarbonate or cAMP-dependent activation of adenylyl cyclase to increase hyphal growth.
source: In C. albicans, CO2 levels are sensed through bicarbonate or cAMP-dependent activation of adenylyl cyclase to increase hyphal growth (Du et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Du et al., 2012 and Hall et al., 2010

claim: Disruption of the RAM pathway effector kinase Cbk1 caused a severe growth defect at host CO2 in C. neoformans but not in C. albicans.
source: We also found that disruption of the RAM pathway effector kinase Cbk1 caused a severe growth defect at host CO2 in C. neoformans but not in C. albicans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: The vast differences between C. neoformans and C. albicans in terms of growth response to CO2 may reflect the evolutionary distance between these species and/or the distinct niches they normally occupy.
source: The vast differences between these organisms in terms of growth response to CO2 may reflect the evolutionary distance between these species and/or the distinct niches they normally occupy.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed differences

claim: C. albicans is a human commensal and has adapted to host CO2 concentrations.
source: Indeed, C. albicans is a human commensal and has adapted to host CO2 concentrations.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: S. cerevisiae is a powerful fermenter that thrives in conditions with high levels of CO2.
source: S. cerevisiae is a powerful fermenter that thrives in conditions with high levels of CO2.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: For the environmental fungus C. neoformans, the ability to grow in a CO2-enriched condition does not appear to be strongly selected for in the natural environment.
source: For the environmental fungus C. neoformans, however, the ability to grow in a CO2-enriched condition does not appear to be strongly selected for in the natural environment, and the host level of CO2 (~5% CO2) is over 100-fold higher than the ambient air (~0.04% CO2).
evidence: Inferred from ecological considerations and CO2 concentration differences

claim: The host level of CO2 (~5% CO2) is over 100-fold higher than the ambient air (~0.04% CO2).
source: For the environmental fungus C. neoformans, however, the ability to grow in a CO2-enriched condition does not appear to be strongly selected for in the natural environment, and the host level of CO2 (~5% CO2) is over 100-fold higher than the ambient air (~0.04% CO2).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of CO2 concentrations

claim: SSD1 is a known suppressor of cbk1Δ phenotypes that has been extensively characterized in ascomycete yeasts to regulate the translation of numerous and diverse mRNA transcripts.
source: While the PARN-encoding gene PSC1 represents an uncharacterized protein, SSD1 is a known suppressor of cbk1Δ phenotypes that has been extensively characterized in ascomycete yeasts to regulate the translation of numerous and diverse mRNA transcripts (Hu et al., 2018; Jansen et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2009b; Wanless et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2018; Jansen et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2009b; and Wanless et al., 2014

claim: In S. cerevisiae, deletion of SSD1 can suppress the lethality of the cbk1Δ mutant but not the cell separation defect, which is regulated by the transcription factor Ace2.
source: Interestingly, in S. cerevisiae, deletion of SSD1 can suppress the lethality of the cbk1Δ mutant but not the cell separation defect, which is regulated by the transcription factor Ace2 (Kurischko et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurischko et al., 2005

claim: In C. albicans, Ssd1 plays an important role in polarized growth and hyphal initiation by negatively regulating the transcription factor Nrg1.
source: In C. albicans, Ssd1 plays an important role in polarized growth and hyphal initiation by negatively regulating the transcription factor Nrg1 (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015

claim: C. neoformans may primarily utilize Ssd1/Psc1 rather than a potential Ace2 homolog to regulate cell separation or polarization.
source: The observation that cbk1Δpsc1Δ and cbk1Δssd1Δ suppressor mutants partially rescue cell separation defects or depolarized growth suggests that C. neoformans may primarily utilize Ssd1/Psc1 rather than a potential Ace2 homolog to regulate cell separation or polarization.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observation that Ssd1/Psc1 mutations rescue cell separation defects

claim: Differential regulation of target mRNA transcripts by Ssd1 and Psc1 may explain the functional divergence of the RAM pathway observed between the basidiomycete Cryptococcus and the ascomycete yeasts.
source: Differential regulation of target mRNA transcripts by Ssd1 and Psc1 may explain the functional divergence of the RAM pathway we observed between the basidiomycete Cryptococcus and the ascomycete yeasts.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed differences

claim: Disruption of Ssd1 and Psc1 suppresses the cbk1Δ mutant's defects at a post-transcriptional level.
source: Our observation that the natural suppressors do not restore transcript abundances of CO2-associated genes in cbk1Δ to WT levels supports a hypothesis that disruption of Ssd1 and Psc1 suppresses the cbk1Δ mutant's defects at a post-transcriptional level.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transcript levels are not restored despite phenotypic rescue

claim: C. neoformans has been demonstrated to use post-transcriptional regulation to adapt to various host stresses.
source: C. neoformans has been demonstrated to use post-transcriptional regulation to adapt to various host stresses (Bloom et al., 2019; Kalem et al., 2021; Stovall et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bloom et al., 2019; Kalem et al., 2021; and Stovall et al., 2021

claim: A temperature-sensitive environmental species of Cryptococcus, Cryptococcus amylolentus, fails to initiate host stress-induced translational reprogramming and is non-pathogenic.
source: A temperature-sensitive environmental species of Cryptococcus, Cryptococcus amylolentus, fails to initiate host stress-induced translational reprogramming and is non-pathogenic (Bloom et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bloom et al., 2019
